news.full_article_text: Audits, SOPs after stormy 2025 season preceded chopper crash near Joshimath Six people died in a Joshimath helicopter crash, renewing concerns over pilgrimage flight safety despite new safeguards in Uttarakhand. Six people were killed after a helicopter crashed near Joshimath in Chamoli district on Friday, adding to a series of accidents in Uttarakhand’s pilgrimage helicopter sector despite successive rounds of safety measures by the aviation regulator. The crash occurred weeks after the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB), in its final report on a fatal 2025 crash in the Kedarnath valley, recommended that pilots complete 50 hours of supervised hill flying before operating alone in the region. The bureau recorded eight accidents and one serious incident in the Char Dham sector between 2015 and 2025. The cause of Friday’s crash is not yet established. Deep Dive The accident is the first in Uttarakhand since the civil aviation ministry introduced sweeping safety measures for the 2026 pilgrimage season. These included air traffic control at Sahastradhara in Dehradun and Sersi in Rudraprayag, command centres monitoring helipads and weather, tracking devices on all helicopters, and ceilometers — instruments that measure cloud-base height — at five locations including Kedarnath and Badrinath. Pilots were required to have at least 750 hours of hill flying, with 100 in the preceding year and 10 take-offs and landings at Kedarnath. Helicopters were barred from filling more than 70% of their passenger capacity. The ministry had said the first phase of the 2026 season passed without incident. The Char Dham sector’s safety record has drawn repeated regulatory intervention. Data the ministry presented in the Rajya Sabha on July 21 last year showed six helicopter accidents during the Char Dham Yatra between 2021 and June 2025, four of them in the first six months of 2025 alone. One accident each was recorded in 2022 and 2023; none in 2021 and 2024. The deadliest recent cluster came in the 2025 season. On May 8, an Aero Trans Services Bell 407 crashed near Gangnani in Uttarkashi after its main rotor struck an overhead fibre-optic cable during a landing attempt, killing six people and seriously injuring another. On May 17, a Pinnacle Air helicopter was involved in an accident near Kedarnath, followed by a Kestrel Aviation helicopter accident at Sersi on June 7. On June 15, an Aryan Aviation Bell 407 flying from Kedarnath to Guptkashi crashed near Gaurikund, killing all seven people on board. The AAIB’s final report on the Gaurikund crash, issued on October 13 this year, identified the pilot’s limited experience of flying in the valley, rapidly descending clouds and the failure to turn back or change course in time among the factors relevant to the accident. It recommended that pilots complete at least 50 hours of supervised dual hill-flying sorties with an experienced pilot before undertaking single-pilot operations in the Kedarnath valley for the first time. It also recommended that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) exercise oversight of the Sitapur control centre and that radio communications between pilots and ground controllers be recorded. In an interim report on the same crash, published in November 2025, investigators had recorded that the Kedarnath valley had no meteorological facility. A weather instrument at the helipad reported wind, visibility and temperature, but provided no information about clouds. Its readings were not stored; a UCADA security staffer shared screenshots on an operators’ WhatsApp group. On the morning of the crash, no weather information had been posted by the time of the first flight. The 2022 Kedarnath crash showed a similar pattern. On October 18 that year, an Aryan Aviation Bell 407 crashed into a mountain ridge near Garud Chatti shortly after taking off from Kedarnath, killing all seven people on board. The AAIB attributed the accident to the crew’s failure to adequately assess deteriorating weather conditions, with fast-descending clouds obscuring visibility. DGCA has responded to accidents with audits, inspections, fines and suspensions. After a hard landing at Kedarnath in June 2022, it audited shuttle operators and fined five of them ₹ 5 lakh each over irregularities in their flying records. After the April 2023 tail-rotor death, it ordered a second audit of all operators before clearing them for the season and announced specialised training for Himalayan flying. Following the 2025 accidents, the regulator ordered special audits, familiarisation flights for pilots new to the sector or returning after more than a year, and deployed air traffic control and meteorological personnel at control rooms in Sahastradhara and Sitapur. The ministry suspended one operator’s Char Dham operations and suspended two pilots’ licences for six months for flying in unsuitable weather. The main rules for pilgrimage flights are set out in an operations circular issued by DGCA in February 2023. For the Kedarnath shuttle, it fixes the route and the altitude at each point: helicopters must climb to 8,500 feet by the valley’s entry and leave it at 9,000 feet on the way back. No more than four helicopters may be in the valley at once. A separate circular on adverse-weather flying, revised on June 12, 2025, requires regular weather updates for the departure point, route and destination, clear criteria for turning back or diverting, a conservative approach to flight decisions, and pilots experienced in bad-weather flying. It prohibits extensions to pilots’ duty hours during the monsoon and requires scenario-based training on diversions. The AAIB states in its reports that the sole objective of its investigations is to prevent accidents, “not to apportion blame or liability”. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Neha LM Tripathi Neha LM Tripathi is a Special Correspondent with the National Political Bureau of Hindustan Times. news.headline: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
news.story_lead: President Volodymyr Zelensky has recently admitted that Ukraine was running critically low on Patriots - Published 15 minutes ago The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks, after Kyiv said deliveries had been delayed in recent months. The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (Â£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly urged the US to speed up deliveries of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
news.full_article_text: President Volodymyr Zelensky has recently admitted that Ukraine was running critically low on Patriots - Published 15 minutes ago The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks, after Kyiv said deliveries had been delayed in recent months. The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (Â£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly urged the US to speed up deliveries of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles. The latest move comes just days after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump, with the US president saying it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to try to end the war with Russia. In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe". It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale". Zelensky said earlier this week that his country had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies. And in a Telegram post late on Friday, the Ukrainian president reported that earlier in the day Russian ballistic missiles had struck two of the country's regions. "They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," he said. Zelensky has recently admitted that Ukraine was running critically low on Patriots, as Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter. Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran. It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine. Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence. In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right. news.headline: Isro's navigation satellite NVS-03 lifts off from Andhra Pradesh's Sriharikota
news.story_lead: Isro's navigation satellite NVS-03 lifts off from Andhra Pradesh's Sriharikota The satellite, which was abroad a GSLV-F18 rocket, had lift off at 11:51pm IST on Friday from the second launch pad of the space centre in Sriharikota. The Indian Space Research Organsiation (Isro) on Friday night launched its navigation satellite NVS-03 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. The satellite, which was abroad a GSLV-F18 rocket had lift off at 11:51pm IST on Friday from the second launch pad of the space centre in Sriharikota.
news.full_article_text: Isro's navigation satellite NVS-03 lifts off from Andhra Pradesh's Sriharikota The satellite, which was abroad a GSLV-F18 rocket, had lift off at 11:51pm IST on Friday from the second launch pad of the space centre in Sriharikota. The Indian Space Research Organsiation (Isro) on Friday night launched its navigation satellite NVS-03 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. The satellite, which was abroad a GSLV-F18 rocket had lift off at 11:51pm IST on Friday from the second launch pad of the space centre in Sriharikota. According to the mission brochure, the targeted orbit for the satellite has a planned perigee (closest point to Earth) of 170 km and an apogee (farthest point) of 37,023 km, at an inclination of 20.75 degrees. Also Read | ISRO to launch NVS-03 satellite on October 30 to boost navigation for trains, vehicles and ships What is NVS-03? NVS-03 is the third, second-generation navigation satellite designed to maintain and boost the continuity of the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) system. With this satellite, the GSLV rocket marks its 20t flight. "Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) is India’s independent regional navigation satellite system designed to provide accurate Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) service to users in India as well as the region extending about 1500 km beyond the Indian landmass, which is its primary service area," said Isro in its brief about the mission. The space organization added that the satellite will carry an indigenous atomic clock, along with the procured atomic clocks. "It will also include a L1 signal in addition to existing L5/S signals with coverage over India land mass and a region extending 1500 km around Indian geopolitical boundary," the statement added further. India's launch of NVS-03 comes as it works towards its own navigation system, which will reduce dependence on the Global Positioning System (GPS), which is currently owned by the US government. Furthermore, the atomic clocks on these satellites give the time as well, which is crucial for banks, stock exchanges and the armed forces, who rely on precise time, and small differences between time sources can affect their operations. This comes after the government announced in 2025 that it would stop using GPS to keep Indian Standard Time and switch to five atomic clocks in Guwahati, Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Faridabad and Bhubaneswar. - Satish Dhawan Space Centre

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) executed the successful launch of the GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission on October 31, 2026.
